--- jupyter: stats --- # Data Processing and EDA This note uses the synthetic [dataset `minidataset.csv`](minidataset.csv) to demonstrate essential data-processing and EDA operations. The dataset contains repeated measurements from several individuals, each with up to three visits. Each row represents one visit for one individual. This note provides brief examples rather than comprehensive instructions for each command. If you choose to use a command in your project, consult its documentation and make sure you apply it appropriately to your data and analysis. ## Load and inspect the data ::: {.cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import pandas as pd df = pd.read_csv("minidataset.csv") df.head() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: The variable `id` identifies the individual, `visit` records the visit number, and `time` records the number of days since baseline. ::: {.cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} print(f"Rows, Columns: {df.shape}") print(f"Individuals: {df['id'].nunique()}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Rows, Columns: (32, 12) Individuals: 12 ``` ::: ::: Count the number of visits recorded for each individual: ::: {.cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} visits_per_id = df.groupby("id").size() visits_per_id.head() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` id 1001 3 1002 3 1003 2 1004 3 1005 3 dtype: int64 ``` ::: ::: Each value is the number of rows, or visits, available for one `id`. ## Merge visits into one row per individual Use `pivot()` to place different visits from the same `id` on one row. To keep the example concise, we select only `num_1` and `num_2`. ::: {.cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} wide = df.pivot(index="id", columns="visit", values=["num_1", "num_2"]) wide.head() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: The result contains one row per individual. ## Avoid data leakage To keep all visits from the same individual together, there are at least two different methods: 1. Reshape the data so that all visits from the same individual appear in one row (using the method mentioned above), and then split by rows. 2. Split the unique IDs and then select their rows. ::: {.cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split ids = df["id"].drop_duplicates() train_ids, remaining_ids = train_test_split(ids, test_size=0.40, random_state=1) val_ids, test_ids = train_test_split(remaining_ids, test_size=0.50, random_state=1) train_df = df.loc[df["id"].isin(train_ids)].copy() val_df = df.loc[df["id"].isin(val_ids)].copy() test_df = df.loc[df["id"].isin(test_ids)].copy() ``` ::: ## Summarize and handle missing values Use `info()` to inspect the data types and non-null count for each column. A non-null count below the total number of rows indicates missing values: ::: {.cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} df.info() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` RangeIndex: 32 entries, 0 to 31 Data columns (total 12 columns): # Column Non-Null Count Dtype --- ------ -------------- ----- 0 id 32 non-null int64 1 visit 32 non-null int64 2 time 32 non-null int64 3 num_1 32 non-null int64 4 cat_1 32 non-null str 5 num_2 32 non-null int64 6 num_3 31 non-null float64 7 num_4 31 non-null float64 8 cat_2 32 non-null int64 9 num_5 32 non-null int64 10 cat_3 32 non-null int64 11 target 32 non-null int64 dtypes: float64(2), int64(9), str(1) memory usage: 3.1 KB ``` ::: ::: For missing values, we could either drop them ::: {.cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} df_dropped = df.dropna() ``` ::: ::: {.callout-caution} Be careful: `dropna()` removes every row that contains at least one missing value. ::: Alternatively, we could use `fillna()` to replace missing values with a specified value, such as $0$: ::: {.cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code} df_filled_0 = df.fillna(0) ``` ::: or we could use `fillna()` to replace missing values with the column mean: ::: {.cell execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code} df_filled = df.copy() df_filled["num_3"] = df_filled["num_3"].fillna(df_filled["num_3"].mean()) ``` ::: Missing values can also be filled with the mean of each group. This example uses the mean within each `cat_1` group: ::: {.cell execution_count=11} ``` {.python .cell-code} df_group_filled = df.copy() group_mean = df.groupby("cat_1")["num_3"].transform("mean") df_group_filled["num_3"] = df_group_filled["num_3"].fillna(group_mean) ``` ::: ::: {.callout-note} ## Imputer The examples above show simple approaches to missing-value imputation. A more complete, cross-validation-safe approach typically combines a `sklearn` imputer with `ColumnTransformer` and `Pipeline`, so that imputation is fitted separately within each training fold and applied consistently to other data. The details of this approach are beyond the scope of this note. ::: ## Construct features Sort by individual and time before calculating within-person differences: ::: {.cell execution_count=12} ``` {.python .cell-code} df_sort = df.sort_values(["id", "time"]).copy() df_sort["time_change"] = df_sort.groupby("id")["time"].diff() df_sort["num_2_change"] = df_sort.groupby("id")["num_2"].diff() df_sort["num_2_change_per_day"] = df_sort["num_2_change"] / (df_sort["time_change"]) df_sort.head() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=12} ```{=html}
